title: Iterative Boolean Summation for Team Implementation
approach_explanation: The solution simulates the decision-making process of the three friends for each of the $n$ problems. For each problem, the views of Petya, Vasya, and Tonya are read as binary inputs. The condition for implementing a problem is that at least two friends must be sure of the solution, which translates to a majority boolean function. The solution computes this condition using a logical expression, accumulates the count of implemented problems, and prints the final total.

code_breakdown.explanation: Reads the number of problems $n$ and initializes a counter variable `problems` to zero.
Iterates $n$ times to process the input for each problem, reading three integer flags $P$, $V$, and $T$ representing the views of Petya, Vasya, and Tonya respectively.

Evaluates whether at least two friends agree using a logical expression. Due to operator precedence nuances in C++, the expression uses a ternary operator to conditionally increment the problem counter.
Prints the total number of problems the team decides to implement to standard output.

complexity_analysis.time_justification: The algorithm loops exactly $N$ times, where $N$ is the number of problems. Inside the loop, constant time $O(1)$ operations (reading three integers, arithmetic evaluation, and conditional increment) are performed. Thus, the total time complexity scales linearly with $N$.
complexity_analysis.space_justification: The algorithm only allocates a few scalar integer variables ($n$, `problems`, $i$, $P$, $V$, $T$) to maintain state regardless of the input size $N$, requiring constant auxiliary space.

strengths: Straightforward simulation logic matching the problem statement directly.
edge_cases_handled: Correctly handles all zero votes and all one votes.
best_practices_feedback: Avoid using operator precedence traps. In the code, `V && T || V&&P || P&&T == 1`, the equality operator `==` has higher precedence than logical operators, which can lead to unexpected logic bugs depending on compiler interpretation.
Using `NULL` in the ternary false branch is poor C++ style; use a no-op statement or simply an `if` statement for clarity.
Include fast I/O optimizations (`ios_base::sync_with_stdio(false); cin.tie(NULL);`) for competitive programming consistency.

optimization_and_alternatives.tradeoffs: Instead of complex boolean expressions with potential operator precedence risks, simply sum the three votes ($P + V + T$) and check if the sum is $\ge 2$. This is cleaner, safer, and easier to maintain.
